paragraphs.heading: Order you can describe
paragraphs.text: A crystal structure is a description of how the atoms, ions or molecules in a crystalline material are laid out in an orderly way. The particles, by their own nature, settle into symmetric patterns that repeat along the main directions of three-dimensional space. Symmetry is the defining property of a crystal: certain symmetry operations leave the lattice looking exactly as it was.

paragraphs.heading: The unit cell
paragraphs.text: The unit cell is the smallest group of particles that makes up the repeating pattern while still carrying the full symmetry of the crystal. Shifting copies of it over and over along its main axes builds the whole crystal, a little like tiles covering a floor. The shifts used to do this mark out points called the nodes of the Bravais lattice.

paragraphs.heading: Six numbers for one box
paragraphs.text: The unit cell has a box-like shape called a parallelepiped. It is pinned down by six lattice parameters: the lengths of its three edges, a, b and c, and the three angles between them, α, β and γ. Particles inside the cell are located by fractional coordinates along its edges, measured from a chosen reference point. In practice only a smallest asymmetric subset, called the asymmetric unit, needs to be listed, since the symmetry operations of the cell produce all the other particles.

paragraphs.heading: Space groups and axes
paragraphs.text: The full set of symmetry operations of a unit cell is written formally as the crystal's space group. Every possible symmetric arrangement of particles in three-dimensional space can be described by 230 space groups. In monoclinic, trigonal, tetragonal and hexagonal systems, one unique principal axis has higher rotational symmetry than the other two, and the plane at right angles to it is called the basal plane. In triclinic, orthorhombic and cubic systems there is no principal axis, and which axis gets which label is arbitrary.

paragraphs.heading: Naming planes with Miller indices
paragraphs.text: Planes and directions in a crystal are named with Miller indices, three numbers written h, k and ℓ. A plane written (hkℓ) crosses the cell axes at a₁/h, a₂/k and a₃/ℓ, or a multiple of these, so the indices scale with the inverses of those crossing points. A zero means the plane never meets that axis. The indices are integers with no common factor, and a negative one is marked with a bar. Angle brackets such as ⟨100⟩ stand for a whole family of directions that symmetry makes equivalent, along with their negatives.

paragraphs.heading: Why the arrangement matters
paragraphs.text: Crystal structure and symmetry strongly shape physical properties, including how a crystal splits, its electronic band structure and whether light passes through it. Cleavage tends to run parallel to planes of higher density, and dislocation glide, part of plastic deformation, prefers such planes too. Adsorption and chemical reactions happen at or near surface particles, so they depend on how densely the nodes are packed.
